title: Zero refresh budget: rewrites of training tensors serve as refresh
idea: Imposed limit: the DRAM may spend zero cycles on refresh. The controller keeps a 2-bit last-written epoch per row, and the training runtime guarantees every activation, gradient and KV buffer is rewritten each step (<20 ms). Rows written within tRET are never refreshed; only a small long-lived bank group holding weights and optimizer state keeps conventional refresh.
why: Fact 3: refresh is 16-33% of idle power and 10-20% of bandwidth. In training, 70-90% of rows are short-lived, so most refresh energy and bandwidth loss disappear.

title: No ECC chip: exponent-only parity carved from mantissa LSBs
idea: Imposed limit: no x72 ECC devices allowed. For bf16/fp8 tensors, the controller reorders bits so the sign and exponent fields of 8 values share one SEC-DED codeword whose check bits are stored in the stolen mantissa LSB of each value. A mantissa flip causes a bounded relative error of under 1%; a catastrophic exponent flip is corrected.
why: Removes the 12.5% ECC device overhead (x72 to x64) and tolerates raw BER ~1e-6 cells, so cheaper or weaker DRAM is usable for AI weights and activations.

title: No counter SRAM: weak canary rows detect row hammer physically
idea: Imposed limit: zero bytes of activation-counter SRAM. Each subarray gets a few sentinel rows built with ~30% smaller storage nodes, so they flip after ~300 neighbor activations. They hold a known pattern, and a comparator checks them during normal refresh. A canary flip raises an alert that triggers targeted refresh of the neighbors.
why: Fact 9: ~1k-activation thresholds need MBs of counter SRAM per channel in counter-based defenses. Canaries cost ~0.1% area and track the same physics automatically as cells get weaker.

title: No digital state: leaky analog activation integrator per wordline driver
idea: Imposed limit: no digital counters or tables anywhere. Each wordline driver gets a tiny MOS capacitor that receives a fixed charge packet on every activation and leaks with a time constant matched to tREFW. When its voltage crosses a comparator threshold, the row latches a neighbor-refresh request that is served at the next RFM slot.
why: Fact 9: exact per-row hammer tracking at ~1k activations becomes ~2 transistors plus 1 capacitor per row driver, with no SRAM, CAM or controller state. It scales to any row count.

title: No Spruce Pine quartz: dirtier wafers paid for with ECC
idea: Imposed limit: no high-purity Spruce Pine crucibles. Grow CZ ingots in synthetic-silica or multiply reused crucibles and accept higher oxygen and metal content, which fattens the retention tail. Compensate with per-die retention fingerprinting, two-rate refresh and a stronger on-die RS code (16-bit symbols per 256 B), turning a purity spec into an ECC budget.
why: Relieves the >80% Spruce Pine chokepoint. A 10x fatter weak-cell tail costs roughly 3% extra capacity in check bits instead of a lost supply chain.

title: Half the voltage: 0.5 V array rescued by on-die BCH
idea: Imposed limit: half the array voltage. Run VARY at ~0.5 V with offset-cancelling sense amplifiers and accept raw BER ~1e-5 from the reduced sense margin. A low-latency on-die BCH(t=2) code per 128 bits, decoded in parallel with column select, cleans up the result.
why: Fact 10 voltage floor: CV^2 array energy falls ~4x at ~6% check-bit overhead and ~1-2 ns decode latency.

title: Zero ECC storage: recompute-from-lineage repairs transient tensors
idea: Imposed limit: no correction bits for transient data. Only a 32-bit CRC per 4 KB is stored, for detection. On a mismatch the runtime re-executes the producing op from its upstream inputs (the op lineage, as in Spark RDDs) within the same step, so recomputation becomes the correction mechanism.
why: Removes 12.5% ECC storage over 60-80% of an AI job's footprint and lets transient tensors live in cheaper, higher-BER DRAM.

title: No per-word ECC: ABFT tile checksums guard weight matrices
idea: Imposed limit: no per-word ECC for weights. Each 128x128 weight tile carries one checksum row and one checksum column, verified for free inside the matmul (Huang-Abraham ABFT). A flipped element is located at the intersection of the failing row and column and corrected from the checksums.
why: Protection overhead falls from 12.5% to ~1.6%, and the checking rides on compute already being done. Weight memory can use non-ECC or raw-BER DRAM.

title: One flag bit: polarity coding keeps weak cells discharged
idea: Imposed limit: one extra bit per 64-bit word. Retention failures happen only when a leaky cell holds its charged state. Using a boot-time weak-cell map, the controller stores either the data or its inverse, whichever puts the known weak cells of that word in their discharged, safe state, and records the choice in the flag bit.
why: Fact 3 retention tail: most weak-cell errors are eliminated at 1.6% overhead, so the refresh interval can stretch 4-8x past the weak tail.

title: 4 ms cells allowed: compressed lines packed around weak bits
idea: Imposed limit: some cells may retain only 4 ms. Each 64 B line is compressed (base-delta or FPC), and the compressed payload is laid out so that the known weak bit positions in that physical line are skipped as don't-care holes. The weak-bit mask comes from a per-row fault map.
why: Rows with dozens of weak cells stay usable at normal refresh rates, so retention-tail binning loss (5-10% of rows) becomes near zero.

title: Half the capacitor: OS-toggled twin-row differential mode
idea: Imposed limit: build cells with half the capacitance (~2.5 fF, AR ~30:1). For pages flagged long-lived, two paired rows are activated together onto complementary bitlines to form a 2T2C differential bit, doubling signal and retention. Short-lived pages run single-ended at full density, and the OS chooses the mode per 2 MB region.
why: Fact 1 charge wall: shorter, cheaper capacitor pillars with fewer etch and deposition steps. Usable density adapts to how much data actually needs long retention.

title: Quarter refresh energy: bit-plane layout refreshes only MSB rows
idea: Imposed limit: refresh energy cut by 75%. The controller transposes int8/fp8 tensors into bit-planes stored in separate rows. MSB-plane rows refresh at the normal rate, and LSB-plane rows refresh 8-16x less often and are allowed to decay.
why: Fact 3: ~60-70% of refresh energy is cut with less than 0.1% model-quality loss for inference weights and activations.

title: No new process step: wordline microheaters anneal leakage traps
idea: Imposed limit: the leakage tail must improve without adding fab steps. Existing wordline and dummy-gate conductors are driven as resistive heaters in maintenance windows (about 1 s pulses heating locally to ~250 C), passivating hydrogen-related interface traps and resetting variable-retention-time defects in the array.
why: Fact 3: shrinking the ≤13 fA tail could let the refresh interval stretch ~4x, plus self-healing of aging-induced leakage over the product's life.

title: No external sensors: ECC syndrome servo trims bias and refresh
idea: Imposed limit: no added test or sense hardware. On-die ECC correction counts per bank feed a closed-loop controller that continuously adjusts the negative wordline voltage, VARY trim and refresh interval to hold a target corrected-error rate (~1e-9). The ECC syndromes are the sensor.
why: Removes worst-case guardbands set for corner temperature and the worst die. Average refresh interval ~2x longer and wordline stress lower.

title: 64-activation cap: hot rows migrate into on-die SRAM
idea: Imposed limit: no row may be activated more than 64 times per refresh window. When a row hits the cap, its contents are copied into a small on-die hot-row SRAM (or a latched spare sense-amp stripe) and served from there for the rest of the window. The DRAM row is never re-opened.
why: Fact 9: row hammer becomes impossible at any threshold above 64, independent of cell weakness, and hot rows also get faster access.

title: Zero added disturb at tighter pitch: buried electron-sink layer
idea: Imposed limit: shrink wordline pitch without adding disturbance. A thin carbon-doped or SiGe trap-rich layer is implanted beneath the buried wordlines. It captures and recombines electrons injected by repeated aggressor activation before they diffuse to neighboring storage-node junctions.
why: Fact 9: could raise hammer thresholds several-fold and allow the 6F^2 pitch to keep shrinking without pushing thresholds below 1k.

title: One retention test only: per-row data whitening kills worst patterns
idea: Imposed limit: testers may screen retention with just one pattern. All data is XORed with a per-row keyed pseudo-random whitening sequence, so worst-case neighbor and bitline-coupling patterns become statistically rare. Refresh and test margins are then set for typical patterns rather than worst-case ones.
why: Cuts retention test time and the pattern-dependent guardband, recovering ~1.5-2x refresh interval and test cost per die.

title: KV cache at one-third cost: range-clamp decoding in gray memory
idea: Imposed limit: KV-cache memory must cost a third as much. The KV cache is stored in gray memory, meaning DRAM run at a 4x refresh interval and low VARY. Instead of parity, per-head statistics (min/max norms) are stored, and any value read outside its head's range is clamped. Attention softmax is robust to sparse bounded flips.
why: Facts 3 and 10: refresh and array energy for the KV cache drop 3-4x, and higher-BER binned dies can serve LLM inference.

title: Twice the bits, same capacitor: trellis-coded four-level cells
idea: Imposed limit: double the bits without a bigger capacitor. Each cell stores 4 charge levels and raw BER of ~1e-3 is accepted. Trellis-coded modulation across 8 cells (as in modems) adds structured redundancy, and the set is decoded by a Viterbi block in the sense-amp periphery.
why: Fact 1 charge wall: ~1.7x net bits per cell after coding overhead with no new capacitor geometry.

title: Zero dies scrapped: AI-tolerant DRAM grade for out-of-spec dies
idea: Imposed limit: no die may be scrapped for retention or margin. Create a new JEDEC-like grade specified at 16 ms retention and BER 1e-8 that requires system-level ECC, recompute or ABFT. It is sold at a ~40% discount into inference clusters whose software stacks tolerate it.
why: Raises usable supply by the 5-15% yield gap at zero capex and relieves the shortage immediately.

title: No EUV: fat DUV cells drop on-die ECC and refresh
idea: Imposed limit: no EUV layers. Use relaxed-pitch DUV cells with ~2x capacitor volume and very low raw BER. On-die ECC (6.25%) is removed and the refresh interval stretched 4x, reclaiming area and bandwidth that partly offset the density loss.
why: Fact 4: removes 5-7 EUV layers from the bill. The reliability margin is spent to claw back ~10% of effective density and ~15% of bandwidth.

title: No tracking state: keyed rotating row permutation defeats hammering
idea: Imposed limit: no per-row tracking state. Each refresh window, the bank rekeys a lightweight Feistel permutation that maps logical to physical rows within a subarray, migrating a few rows per refresh command. An attacker cannot keep hammering the same physical neighbors long enough to cause a flip.
why: Fact 9: probabilistic hammer immunity at near-zero area; cost is ~1-2% extra row copies during refresh.

title: Zero added read latency: optimistic CRC read, lazy LDPC correction
idea: Imposed limit: ECC may add zero read latency. Data returns immediately with a 1-cycle CRC check, and the core speculates on it. On a CRC failure the pipeline squashes, and a strong flash-style LDPC decoder (~200 ns) corrects the line from a long codeword spanning 4 lines.
why: Flash-class codes become usable in DRAM, tolerating raw BER ~1e-4 cells (cheaper, denser, lower voltage) with no average latency penalty.

title: Never discard: modules shrink capacity gracefully as spares run out
idea: Rule: no module is ever thrown away for errors. Firmware consumes spare rows via soft PPR. When spares are exhausted, it offlines failing 2 MB regions and advertises reduced capacity through CXL dynamic capacity, and the OS migrates pages away. End-of-life modules are resold at their measured remaining capacity.
why: Extends module life ~2x and keeps ~95% of a module's bits in service instead of discarding 100% at the first uncorrectable error.

title: Die passport: on-die ledger makes recycled DRAM cheap to re-bin
idea: Rule: every die must be recyclable without full re-test. Each die carries a few-kB OTP or MRAM ledger recording its retention map, measured hammer threshold, PPR repairs, temperature history and error counts. Refurbishers read the ledger in seconds to re-bin and re-sell the die.
why: Re-test cost (the main barrier to DRAM reuse) drops ~80%, making second-life dies economical and raising usable supply.

title: Reworkable HBM: low-melt indium bumps let bad dies be swapped
idea: Rule: an HBM stack must be repairable at die level. Core dies are stacked with indium or Sn-Bi microbumps that reflow at ~120-140 C instead of permanent hybrid bonds, so a die that fails at stack test or in the field can be desoldered and replaced at a repair station.
why: Fact 6: much of the 20-30% HBM stack yield loss becomes a die swap rather than scrapping 8-12 good dies.

title: Hot-swap CXL memory bricks with erasure-coded striping
idea: Rule: any memory unit must be removable for repair while the system runs. Pages are striped with RS(8+2) across 10 CXL memory bricks, so any brick can be pulled live, repaired or replaced, and rebuilt in the background onto a hot spare.
why: Tolerates whole-device failure at 20% overhead. Lets cheap, unqualified or second-life DRAM serve production pools, raising usable supply.

title: Rewritable repair maps in on-die MRAM replace laser fuses
idea: Rule: repairs must be redoable for the whole life of the part. One-time laser and e-fuse redundancy is replaced by a small on-die MRAM or FeFET repair table, so row and column remapping can be revised any number of times in the field and again at refurbishment, including undoing a repair onto a spare that later fails.
why: Turns redundancy from a one-shot fab resource into a lifelong repair budget, raising field survival and second-life yield.

title: Second-life DRAM harvested from retired AI servers
idea: Rule: no retired DRAM goes to shredding. An industrial line desolders DRAM packages from 4-5-year-old hyperscaler boards, grades them with BIST, reballs them and assembles new modules with chipkill and stronger ECC for tier-2 CXL expansion memory, priced at 30-50% of new.
why: Adds supply equal to a fraction of annual fleet retirements at near-zero fab capex. Also raises U.S. manufacturability, because the work is assembly and test rather than wafer fabrication.

title: Diels-Alder reversible mold compound for intact die recovery
idea: Rule: the package must open without damaging the die. DRAM is encapsulated in a mold compound with thermally reversible Diels-Alder crosslinks that de-crosslink at ~150 C, so dies can be lifted intact from failed or retired packages for failure analysis, repair or repackaging.
why: Makes die-level recycling and failure analysis cheap. Recovered good dies add supply, and the root-cause loop for reliability shortens.

title: Electrical healing: scheduled BTI recovery epochs for aged periphery
idea: Rule: repair by electricity, not replacement. The controller schedules recovery epochs that apply reverse gate bias and modest self-heating to sense-amp and wordline-driver transistors, reversing accumulated BTI threshold shifts that erode sense margin over years.
why: Keeps aged modules within margin for second and third service lives, so fewer are retired for slow parametric drift.

title: Partial-good HBM: channel-isolated stacks sold and run degraded
idea: Rule: a dead channel must not kill a stack. Each HBM pseudo-channel gets independent power gating and fuse-isolatable TSV groups, so stacks with failed channels ship as 75% or 50% capacity SKUs, and channels that fail in the field are fenced off instead of retiring the stack.
why: Fact 6: recovers much of the 20-30% stack yield loss as sellable bits and lengthens field life.

title: Socketed DRAM chiplets on a reusable multi-generation interposer
idea: Rule: memory dies must be replaceable without discarding logic. DRAM chiplets attach to an active interposer through anisotropic conductive film or micro-spring contacts instead of permanent bonds, so failed chiplets are swapped and the interposer and accelerator are reused across 2-3 memory generations.
why: Cuts scrap of expensive packages from a single memory failure. Interposer capital is amortized across generations.

title: U.S. memory remanufacturing depots instead of new fabs
idea: Rule: failed memory must be repaired, not replaced. Regional U.S. depots equipped with testers, PPR programmers, die-rework and reball lines receive failed modules from hyperscalers. Most failures are a single die or row, so modules are repaired and returned within days.
why: Raises U.S. manufacturability and value-add without a $15B fab. Each repaired module is supply that does not need a new wafer.

title: Serviceable-memory procurement rule with open error-log standard
idea: Rule: policy must force repairability. Federal and large-buyer procurement requires socketed or CAMM-style memory and an open JEDEC-style error-log interface (per-row correction counts, PPR history), so memory can be diagnosed, repaired and moved between devices instead of soldered and scrapped.
why: Expands the reusable memory pool and creates demand for repair telemetry. Reduces e-waste of soldered DRAM.

title: Self-repairing TSV mesh with spare vias and in-stack switches
idea: Rule: interconnect failures must heal in the field. Stacks include ~10% spare TSVs plus tiny per-die crossbar switches. In-field BIST detects TSVs degrading from electromigration or cracking and reroutes their signals to spares without removing the stack.
why: Fact 6: lowers stack yield loss and field returns from TSV defects, extending stack life.

title: Memory leasing with telemetry-driven swap and refurbishment
idea: Rule: the maker keeps ownership, so repairability is its own profit motive. Memory is leased by GB-month, and the vendor monitors error telemetry, swaps degrading modules proactively, then refurbishes and redeploys them, which rewards designs that last.
why: Aligns the business model with longevity. Each module serves 2-3 deployments, which multiplies supply per wafer.

title: Aging-adaptive ECC: code strength rises as the module ages
idea: Rule: an aging module is re-formatted, never retired. Modules start life with light ECC to maximize capacity. As per-region error rates climb, firmware re-encodes regions into stronger codes (SEC-DED, then RS t=2, then t=4), trading capacity for reliability. Second-life buyers get a matured, highly reliable module at lower capacity.
why: Gives more bits early in life and extends usable life far beyond one fixed-code design.

title: Replaceable base die carries ECC and refresh logic upgrades
idea: Rule: reliability logic must be upgradable without scrapping arrays. In stacked DRAM, the ECC engines, refresh scheduler, hammer defense and repair logic live in a base die joined through a reworkable interface. When better algorithms appear, the base die is swapped and the array dies are reused.
why: Fact 7: periphery (~49% of die) moves to a cheap logic node. Arrays outlive several generations of reliability logic.

title: Field-patchable row-hammer defense in an embedded FPGA buffer
idea: Rule: a new attack must never force a recall. Row-hammer mitigation runs in a small eFPGA or microcode engine in the RCD/CXL buffer, so new defenses against new attack variants can be patched over the air instead of discarding vulnerable modules.
why: Fact 9: avoids fleet-wide module replacement when thresholds drop or new attacks appear, keeping deployed DRAM in service.

title: Fleet-learned repair: OTA refresh and PPR updates by lot signature
idea: Rule: repair must reach modules already in the field. The vendor aggregates anonymized ECC logs from millions of modules, learns failure signatures per wafer lot, and pushes firmware updates that adjust refresh rates and run pre-emptive soft PPR on modules carrying the same lot ID before they fail.
why: Turns field reliability into a continuously improving software problem and cuts uncorrectable-error returns.

title: Spare subarray swap triggered by ECC error-trend detection
idea: Rule: big defects must be fixable in place. Each bank holds one spare subarray (~1/64). When ECC logs show a subarray's error rate trending upward (for example, a failing sense-amp stripe), it is copied into the spare with in-DRAM bulk row copy and remapped live.
why: Repairs large-area defects that spare rows cannot cover at ~1.5% area, so fewer modules are retired.

title: Deuterium-passivated cells with depot re-deuteration window
idea: Rule: the retention tail must be restorable at refurbishment. Interfaces are passivated with deuterium instead of hydrogen, using the stronger Si-D bond for slower trap generation. The package includes a gas-permeable window so depots can re-deuterate aged dies in a long, low-temperature D2 soak (~200 C).
why: Fact 3: a slower-growing, restorable leakage tail allows longer refresh intervals over the life of the part and more service lives.

title: N+1 hot-spare die inside every DRAM package
idea: Rule: a dead die must be fenced and replaced in situ. Each multi-die package carries one spare die behind in-package switches. When a die fails, its contents are rebuilt from chipkill parity onto the spare and the failed die is disconnected.
why: Package survives the first die failure at ~1/N capacity overhead, and the package and module get far longer field lives.

title: Undiced wafer-scale DRAM panel that maps out failing tiles
idea: Rule: defects are routed around, never scrapped. DRAM stays as an undiced wafer of tiles linked by a mesh network. Defective tiles are mapped out at test and in the field, and when enough tiles fail, the panel moves to a lower service tier rather than being discarded.
why: Eliminates die-level yield loss, dicing and packaging, and gives a gradual decline in capacity rather than a sudden end of life.

title: Latent TSV stubs let retired DDR dies become HBM stacks
idea: Rule: every die must have a higher-value second life. DDR dies are designed with TSV keep-out zones and buried, unrevealed TSV stubs. Retired dies are thinned, revealed and stacked into low-cost HBM-like stacks for second-life inference memory.
why: Fact 6: turns retired commodity bits into scarce stacked bandwidth without new wafers.
